This study presents a novel time-changing regression model called Temporal-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous terms, suitable for analyzing count-based data with complex dynamic relationships. Our research indicates that our TV-PAREX model can be estimated efficiently using an EM-based algorithm, ensuring parameter stability. We also developed an R package, tvparex, providing a user-friendly interface for applying the TV-PAREG model in real-world scenarios. The package is available at https://github.com/CRAN/tvparex.

While using stellar photometry to monitor aerosols may seem like a novel concept, its applications are rapidly evolving. Recent developments include the creation of a new parameter called angular scattering measure (AM) which provides more precise information about aerosols than angular radius ($\theta$). This new metric allows for more accurate retrievals of aerosol depth (AAOD) and overall optical depth (AOD) by accounting for aerosol height and angular scattering patterns. As a result, stellar photometry can now effectively observe thin aerosol layers and even separate aerosol and cloud optical depths. Additionally, this new approach enables the creation of high-resolution aerosol maps and allows for the simultaneous retrieval of aerosol height and type by combining stellar and space-based optical depth data. With multiple stellar satellites set to launch in the near future, there is a growing need to standardize and develop new data products to fully utilize this new technology.

Numerous configurational molecular sampling methods such as molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo techniques have their respective strengths and weaknesses. Despite the popularity of Nos\'e-Hoover chain (NHC) and its chain length 1 variant, recent studies have highlighted the precise conditions necessary for these methods to conserve exact configurational integrity. Additionally, their stability can be challenged by complex potentials and thermostatting schemes. In contrast, NHC is misinterpreted as violating configurational conservation, yet this discrepancy can be rectified by revisiting the theoretical underpinnings. A novel understanding has emerged, accurately explaining the precise mechanisms behind NHC's performance. Building on this comprehension, a modified NHC variant, along with an existing method, can sample complex molecular configurations effectively and efficiently, especially when incorporating electric fields. Its code is available at https://github.com/ChimeraPhysics/chimera++

Recent advances in image description techniques have yielded methods capable of generating text summaries of images, although the accuracy of these approaches varies. To evaluate the effectiveness of these methods, there is a need for a standard and reliable evaluation framework, which currently relies on human-generated descriptions. In contrast to human descriptions, automated techniques may improve over time, reducing the reliance on costly and time-consuming human assessment. We propose a novel concept: using automated image descriptions as a reference standard for evaluating evaluation metrics. This proposal involves recalculating previously obtained results using the newly acquired data and exploring new evaluation strategies. We collected large datasets of human-approved image descriptions and conducted an in-depth analysis of existing evaluation metrics, along with several new metrics, to determine what contributes to the variability in performance. As a result, we identified conditions under which certain metrics perform better than others and established guidelines for choosing the most appropriate metrics for use with image description techniques.

We use the concept of conformal field theory and its relationship with Euler-Arnold equations to explore new perspectives on its conditions and observable phenomena. A comprehensive analysis of the equation's implications begins with an in-depth examination of the Virasoro algebra's central extension requirements, followed by an investigation of its relevance to minimal models, the state equation, and the conformal anomaly's origin. Additionally, we explore how Fuchsian representations of the Euler-Arnold equation's operator $K$ are related to CFT, which enables us to map its Casimir operators to convergent series of Virasoro generators. The study's outcomes contribute to a deeper understanding of CFT conditions and observable phenomena, which can be applied across a broad spectrum of research areas, including string theory, 2D gravity models, and certain statistical physics phenomena.

Predictions from high-energy collisions involving heavy ions and protons/proton beams are typically based on relativistic quantum field theories, specifically perturbative QCD and its extension to next-to-leading order. While these predictions are accurate for light flavor particles, they are not suitable for heavy quarks as they rely on existing hadron masses and their lack of formation times. A theoretical framework that accounts for hadron formation times is necessary for heavy flavor particles, which is fulfilled by statistical hadronization models such as Smith-Schachter-Thaler (SST) and its thermal extension. A recent study involving heavy-ion and proton-proton collisions at the LHC has led to forecasts for additional heavy baryons and mesons that could be discovered by the LHCb experiment or a future electron-proton collider. These predictions are anticipated to contribute significantly towards a comprehensive list of heavy particle forecasts.

This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents for the wideband waveforming scheme proposed in [1], which utilizes combined data and power transmission. The proposed optimal wideband waveforming policy for multiple input/output (MISO) systems with multiple carriers (MC-OFDM) involves distributing power across carriers and antennas to maximize signal-to-noise ratio, thereby determining the optimal transmission strategy. The optimal policy for the single-input/single-output (SISO) case with a single carrier is also included, as well as the derivation of achievable rates using fixed points.

Integrating vast amounts of data from experiments in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions is the purpose of our proposed theoretical framework, which is designed to fit current proton phase space density estimates. Unlike previous attempts, our approach accounts for underlying events in proton-proton collisions and meets the requirements of consistency, uniqueness, and determinism. The framework's uniqueness guarantee ensures that fitting the data for proton phase space density estimates and fitting the data for nucleon navigation charts are computationally feasible and meet the requirements mentioned above. A script has been provided to facilitate the implementation of our framework, which can be further modified to fit additional data. The Mathematica code used to develop the framework is available for download at dx.doi.org/10.21221/mmath 00004.

This study employs an active flame method within a linearized Eulerian-Lagrange framework to predict how turbulent jet fires react to acoustic oscillations, specifically exploring the role of flame instability in their behavior, as well as the impact of chemical reactions on flame dynamics, by analyzing the interaction between jets and obstacles. A parallel computing environment was utilized to run the simulations on a highly complex geometry, reducing the need for simplifying assumptions about the initial conditions or the role of flame instability. The results show that the growth of flames in narrow passages can be attributed to the amplification of velocity fluctuations in response to acoustic oscillations, rather than flame instability, and that the transfer of energy from acoustic waves to fluctuations occurs rapidly.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on the description of gravity as a mass energy relation, this new approach bypasses the need for a gravitational field tensor. The fundamental components of the nonlocal gravity framework, specifically the essential tetrads and constitutive connections, are explored in this study. A key aspect of this paper is the derivation of the constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity, a key component that was initially unknown. The research also extends the nonlocal gravity theory to a polynomial version, incorporating the description of a polynomial nonlocal gravity model. A polynomial nonlocal gravity model can be applied to various astronomical events, such as supernovae explosions, a subject of controversy among scientists.

This paper presents a comprehensive overview of minor systems, which refer to hadronic interactions resulting in final states containing only a few particles, potentially exploitable for discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model, using the Large Hadron Collider data. A detailed examination of minor systems is crucial for developing an effective search strategy for new physics, particularly in scenarios where production mechanisms deviate from predicted outcomes or involve invisible particles. We examine various minor systems, including W-photon, top-photon, vector boson scattering, Higgs boson decays to invisible particles, and the production of hidden sectors through entangled particle decays. A discussion of key issues, such as signal identification, background suppression, and new physics signatures, is also provided.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of neutron star binary systems in the region. A crucial aspect of these systems is the recurrence period of X-ray transients, which can provide valuable information on the mass of the neutron star. However, determining this period for most sources is challenging due to a lack of data. To address this issue, we examined a comprehensive list of neutron star binary systems discovered through X-ray transients and compared the period distribution of known and unknown recurrence periods. Our research reveals that a significant fraction of low-mass X-ray transients in the Galactic Centre likely have recurrence periods exceeding a decade for most systems and a majority of outbursts go undetected. Consequently, a substantial portion of previously undiscovered AXP and SXP binaries probably exist within the region, which may resemble a dense population of systems similar to the Monoceros Inner Canon observed through hydrogen alpha emission.

Given a bipartite graph B = (U $\cup$ V, E), the Bipartite Vertex Partition problem seeks the minimum number of parts required to partition sets U and V, with each edge connecting a node from U to a node in V in a subset of edges of B. We present a polynomial-time algorithm that solves BVDP in FPT time, with the parameter being the maximum degree of the graph.

As CPU frequencies continue to increase, power consumption has become a pressing concern. Despite this, current CPUs often operate well beyond the optimal frequency for many workloads, leading to unnecessary energy waste. This research seeks to address this issue by introducing HyperDegrade, a novel architecture that dynamically adjusts CPU frequencies at the granularity of individual cores. HyperDegrade's design features a two-tiered frequency hierarchy, with a high-bandwidth low-latency memory interface connecting the high-speed core to a slower companion core. By offloading majority of the workload to the companion core, HyperDegrade enables the implementation of aggressive frequency scaling without compromising performance. The results show that HyperDegrade outperforms existing approaches by an average of 2.4 times in terms of performance per watt and 3.8 times in terms of average frequency, further demonstrates the potential of a hyper-speed slowness design where the fast core operates at 3.2 GHz and the slow core at 800 MHz, and successfully integrates HyperDegrade with a popular deep learning framework, achieving significant performance boosts without noticeable slowdowns.

A new algorithm called "Peel$^2$" has been developed for untangling knots in classical and welded knots. Although a straight forward application of Peel$^2$ to untangle a knot appears complicated, modifying the problem by introducing points of change has significantly simplified the process. In the category of welded knots, this new procedure has an efficiency of about 0.8, which is a measure of how directly the algorithm untangles the knot without requiring further simplification. A key advantage of Peel$^2$ is that it introduces points of change minimally, which is crucial for further use in applications. Building upon Peel$^2$, a new record of all-time high efficiency of 0.83 was achieved by the "Peel$^2$ + Resolution" algorithm, which combines the current method with the well-established resolution procedure.

In collaborative tasks, multiple robots are assigned areas to scan and share data to achieve a goal. The efficiency of this process can be improved by optimizing the areas each robot investigates and the information they exchange. This study investigates an efficient strategy for this purpose, using a basic algorithm that only requires limited computation and communication capabilities. The proposed method ensures each robot performs the most valuable task at the current time, in the most informed way, in order to maximize the overall outcome. In return, a simple communication action is required. The research finds that this optimal approach is unattainable in most situations due to its complex nature. However, it is possible to approximate the ideal outcome by using a proven existing method. In return, a simple computation and communication process is necessary. A more complex approach yields a more precise outcome but at a higher cost. The research finds that the optimal approach is hard to achieve on most networks but can be feasible on linear networks. A more complex approach is also hard to achieve on most networks but possible on linear networks.

In this study, we extend the concept of representing a group through a wreath product in several areas of mathematics, including group theory, combinatoratorics, and statistical physics. Previously, a straightforward approach was employed to compute the wreath products of finite groups, specifically for pairs of groups G and H. We replace the previous method with the Cartesian Partition Approach, highlighting the advantages of this new approach over the previous one. Furthermore, we explore various applications of the Cartesian Partition Approach in several representation scenarios, involving multiple groups and their composite representations, as well as analyzing the computation of $\operatorname{alt}\pi$, the alternating representation of a pie-shaped representation scheme $\pi$.

Optical interferometers at the heart of ground-based gravitational wave detectors experience non-linear frequency response, particularly when sensing mass variations. This issue is most pronounced for low-frequency motions of the mirror, which can cause problems for future detectors planned to detect gravitational waves of higher frequency. To address this challenge, a new interferometer design called the sloshing-Sagnac topology is proposed, which modifies the optical layout by introducing an additional mirror that creates an additional optical path. By adjusting the angle of the additional mirror, the kernel of the signal output can be intentionally made non-optimal for the standard picture of interferometer dynamics, thereby improving the response of the detector to low-frequency gravitational waves. Based on basic parameters, it is predicted that this enhanced design could outperform the current signal-output kernel when detecting gravitational waves of high frequency, with some variations in performance depending on the specific design.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems using stochastic access protocols have a promising future for widespread adoption. To further the development of such systems and understand their potential in crowded spaces like public venues, a precise analysis of visibility areas is crucial. In a process where devices are randomly positioned within a square area, researchers found that a significant portion of the space remains uncovered by the signal from certain devices, even when transmission powers are maximized. Contrary to similar large-scale systems, a unique phenomenon occurred where certain areas within the perimeter of the square remained outside the range of detection from nearby devices. The unanswered questions surrounding the maximum possible areas of this effect spurred the current investigation. After applying complex calculations, researchers discovered an unknown formula for the maximum possible non-overlapping areas in square-shaped areas with large-scale MIMO systems. The findings offer several possible applications, including the optimization of signal strength, the design of communication protocols, and the use of space in crowded areas.

Neural text creation systems have revolutionized language generation, especially since the emergence of big data and the development of neural language models. However, recent research indicates that $n$-gram models, which were surpassed by neural models, are still highly effective, particularly when employed as a base layer in neural networks. This discovery prompts an investigation into the potential source of $n$-gram models' success and their possible integration into neural models through a residual learning approach. Our findings reveal that $n$-gram models possess valuable knowledge that neural models lack, specifically in predicting rare word sequences. By incorporating a $3$-gram base layer, we enhance the performance of a neural model, demonstrating significant gains in language modeling tasks on widely used datasets, including Wikipedia and the Internet. These outcomes suggest a new perspective on language model creation, emphasizing the significance of $n$-gram models as a foundation for neural models to build upon.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed Optical Recognition of hand-marked paper ballot symbols, with a focus on determining accurate counts of election outcomes, as an alternative to Mark Sense Audio assistance for voters with disabilities, particularly those who require assistance with voting due to a disability.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an idealized atmosphere with a rapidly rotating and insulating sphere, similar to Jupiter or gas giants. To better understand how circulation patterns form and change under different rotational speeds and temperature conditions, multiple scenarios with varying parameters are examined. The results show that extreme fast rotation around the mid-latitudes leads to extremely strong westward wind speeds at high altitudes, similar to giant planet atmosphere behavior, and that increased rotation time reduces atmospheric heat distribution fairness. Reduced rotation around the equator enhances eastward wind speeds and decreases westward wind speeds at the poles. Faster cooling around the equator enhances eastward wind forces and decreases westward wind forces at the poles. Weak atmospheric friction allows higher low-pressure area pressure at the poles and lower pressure at the equator, and stronger friction has the opposite effect. Extremely strong rotation around the equator reduces atmospheric heat distribution fairness in the troposphere and increases it in the stratosphere. Extremely weak friction reduces atmospheric heat distribution unfairness in the troposphere and increases it in the stratosphere. Extremely strong rotation around the equator reduces atmospheric heat circulation at the poles and increases it at the mid-latitudes, and stronger friction has the opposite effect.

This study formulates a range of integral representations for the reciprocal gamma function, utilizing a parameterizing approach to redefine the function in the form of a ratio. This redefined function serves as a basis for constructing a series of integral expressions in various forms, each with distinct weighting functions. The process involves applying the redefined function to a change-of-variable technique, followed by the use of partial fractions to split the function into multiple components, which can then be integrated once each. The resulting expressions for the reciprocal gamma function may be utilized in the calculation of its products, given its ratio-based definition.

Researchers have developed a hydrodynamic theory for Bose fluids, encompassing both condensate and non-condensate phases, in a fully quantum context. This novel approach extends previous hydrodynamic methods, overcoming limitations associated with the OEM and OGEM descriptions of collective excitations. Theoretical foundations have been established for both the linear and nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations, enabling the description of the dynamics of Bose fluids in a fully quantum level. This quantum hydrodynamic theory can be applied to investigate various phenomena, including the onset of non-equilibrium situations, the development of condensate fragmentation, and the dynamics of phase transitions. Theoretical frameworks have been compared and contrasted, highlighting their unique characteristics, particularly in a single-dimensional harmonic trap scenario. The phase-space hydrodynamic theory demonstrates its effectiveness in analyzing short-time non-equilibrium dynamics, while the linearized equation can be employed to examine long-time equilibrium properties. Theoretical predictions have been validated through the development of a linearized quantum hydrodynamic theory, employing a Gaussian approximation for the Wigner function. The most sophisticated phase-space hydrodynamic description has been applied to investigate the collapse of Bose-Einstein condensates in a 3D free space scenario, overcoming limitations associated with existing OEM and OGEM analyses.

This paper provides a comprehensive review of the Educator-Pupil framework, which is designed to facilitate the learning process by teaching the neural network how to perform a particular task before training, thus reducing the need for a large dataset. We examine the various methods that have utilized the Educator-Pupil framework for knowledge acquisition, focusing on instruction design, learning objectives, and the types of tasks that can be learned. We also investigate the theoretical aspects of the framework, delving into concepts such as overfitting, optimization algorithms, and robustness. Furthermore, we discuss the practical applications of the Educator-Pupil framework, analyzing how it can be employed for multi-task learning, learning from scratch, and utilizing external knowledge. We also examine the latest developments in the field, including the use of pre-trained models, few-shot learning, and adaptive models. Finally, we outline promising directions for future research, including the utilization of the framework for understanding deep learning models, improving model explainability, and exploring the theoretical foundations of the framework.

We introduce a new approach, which we call a Brief Function, that significantly accelerates the exact computation of Marginally Exact Probabilities, as well as meets the needs of various constrained optimization problems within graphical models. Our method builds upon recent advances by Han and Yalcin, and specifically extends their Brief Function to accommodate complex models and objective functions. The Brief Function's key innovation is the use of a single, all-purpose function that can be evaluated at multiple points with minimal computational overhead, in contrast to previous methods that use a separate function for each point. We prove the theoretical correctness of our Brief Function-based algorithms and provide a wide range of numerical examples demonstrating their substantial performance improvements over current methods.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Furthermore, a higher rank variant known as the special Askey-Wilson algebra $(sAW)_3$ is found to be isomorphic with the centralizer $Z_3(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through the aforementioned approach, thereby providing an novel insight into its structure as well.

The structured test statistic, particularly the paired-permutation test in NLP tasks, relies heavily on exact, naive calculation methods for its permutation distribution. Due to the complexity of modern models and the increasing size of language datasets, this methodology is no longer feasible for precise paired-permutation examination. To address this challenge, an efficient algorithm called Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PPPE) is proposed, based on existing precise structured permutation techniques. The key improvement lies in modifying the current implementation to accommodate paired data, thereby reducing computational burdens. The proposed PPPE approach achieves this through a refined analysis of paired data, drawing on existing discrete global approximation methods for initial ballpark estimates, followed by a more precise calculation using a Poisson approximation. The proposed method has several advantages over existing alternatives, primarily due to its ability to provide exact results without the need for post-processing adjustment, thereby eliminating discrepancies caused by using different approximation methods. The proposed technique is particularly valuable for Scalding's HypoTestStats library, which experiences significant performance issues with modern NGLM models on large language datasets. The proposed PPPE approach demonstrates a significant improvement over current precise structured permutation methods for paired tests, reducing computation time substantially in various benchmark tests on a range of NGLM models and datasets.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study presents a modified Particle Meta Bayesian Measures filter known as the g-PMBB filter, which incorporates a partially grid-based Bayesian birth model. The filter's effectiveness is demonstrated by applying it to a system with an unknown number of targets and using data from sensors that are not uniformly distributed across the area of interest. Unlike traditional Bayesian birth models, the partially grid-based approach presented here accounts for the presence of areas where no new target sightings occur, which can provide valuable information about the dynamics of the environment. A key advantage of this g-PMBB filter is that it can be used to determine the optimal placement of sensors to maximize the amount of information gained from their data, which has important implications for sensor network planning, particularly in environments where sensors are limited or expensive to deploy.

The structure of soccer matches is unpredictable, with outcomes frequently decided in the final minutes of play. This paper examines the use of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithms in pivotal situations on the soccer field, with the objective of developing tactics that increase the probability of scoring and drawing, as well as reducing the risk of conceding, based on historical UEFA Champions League data. Our optimized policy in high-stakes situations on the ball results in higher expected outcomes compared to standard policies, with better scores achieved by players who possess more skill and are in a more advantageous position, although the enhancement is more notable for more skilled players and those in more advantageous positions. Furthermore, our analysis finds that the DQN algorithm overestimates the value of policy evaluations in these situations, leading to inaccurate decision-making, whereas the DPG algorithm provides more accurate evaluations.

The development of optical systems for velocity field measurements is often hampered by the limitations of probe positioning and the time-consuming process of setting up multiple-component laser diode systems. This research addresses these challenges by presenting a novel technique where a single-component LIDV system with a scanning mechanism is used to obtain two-dimensional velocity vector maps. The proposed method relies on the application of stereo triangulation to calculate the 3D position of the measurement point, allowing the creation of a 2D velocity vector map by simply adjusting the scanning angle of the probe. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated by conducting experiments using a Blasius boundary layer flow and a turbulent flow over a backward-facing step, with results compared to time-resolving PIV data to validate the technique's accuracy. The research findings suggest that this single-point LIDV method can accurately measure two-dimensional velocity vector maps, with minor errors in velocity magnitude measurements.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, hidden light bosons can be difficult to detect if they escape detection by interacting with the detector or a nearby material. This issue is particularly pronounced in searches for axion-like particles (ALPs), as their low mass may lead to elusive behavior. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed an innovative approach, using the decay of $B$ mesons into two photons as a means to search for ALPs. By analyzing how ALPs affect the angle at which these photons are emitted, scientists can identify patterns that indicate the presence of ALPs, even if they have already left the detector or a nearby material. This method allows the search for ALPs in $B$ decay experiments to be more effective, drawing comparisons with existing searches and illustrating the potential for discovering ALPs with low masses by the Belle II experiment.

Recent advances in language frameworks such as BERT and its variants have led to their application in analyzing vocabulary evolution and changes in word meanings. Our investigations utilizing these contextualized language models on a dataset revealing English word semantic shifts showed promising results in mapping words with evolving meanings. Notably, we observed strong associations between semantic changes and shifts in contextualized embeddings. In cases where meaningful differences were noted, further analysis revealed correlations with various aspects of word sense evolution. Our findings suggest that contextualized language models can effectively identify words experiencing meaning shifts, primarily when considering periods of significant change. To contribute to the development of a dictionary tracking semantic changes, we propose an approach using contextualized embeddings to accurately identify words with evolving meanings. Words thus identified could serve as a foundation for mapping shifts in word meanings, thereby informing the creation of a dynamic dictionary.

Remarkably large spins have been observed in a few massive quasars, which could be indicated by the presence of ultralight bosons, such as axions or sterile neutrinos, through the mechanism of instabilities in black hole disks. To confirm this possibility, we examine the relationship between the observed spins and the characteristics of these ultralight bosons. Specifically, we investigate the minimum mass of these bosons that would explain the exceptionally large spins of these quasars, as well as their minimum Compton wavelength, by analyzing the stability of disk spins around black holes. Our findings suggest that an ultralight scalar composite, similar to axion-like particles, with a mass in the range of $10^{-21}$ to $10^{-20}$ electron volts, would be sufficient to account for the large spins observed in these quasars, by preventing the growth of high-frequency gravitational wave modes through the same mechanism of spin instability. Moreover, we propose that future observations of the spin rates of these quasars, as well as the properties of ultralight bosons, could be investigated through the analysis of X-ray variability, which would provide more precise information on the spins of these quasars, potentially leading to the discovery of ultralight bosons.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation methods. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare calculus to accommodate expectations, modifying the original logic to suit our settings and incorporating the notion of relations. This reformulated calculus consists of three parts: the basic Hoare calculus, the quantum relational Hoare calculus, and the quantum calculus with relations and expectations, each requiring a unique proof strategy. We have further developed a formal definition of the calculator with the capability to evaluate programs that utilize relational functions under the formulation with expectations, incorporating a semantics for the calculator and a validation procedure for validators.

The use of machine learning algorithms to analyze solar images has led to a plethora of data on magnetic fields, which in turn requires precise measurement of vector magnetic fields. However, current spectropolarimetric instruments can only directly determine the strength and direction of these fields for certain wavelengths, leading to various inference methods to obtain more information. Recently, researchers have reported biases in vector magnetic field measurements derived from Helioseismics and Magnetic Field (HMI) data, which has sparked concern about the reliability of these measurements. In a study published in Physical Review Research, researchers found that noise in the measured intensities affects the accuracy of vector magnetic field mappings, with biases appearing in certain areas with intense magnetic fields. To address this issue, a new method has been proposed that accounts for noisy signal-to-noise ratios at the expense of resolving the underlying cause of the noise. However, in a different study, researchers found that the new method overestimates the noise, leading to biased magnetic field mappings. To better understand these findings, additional research is necessary to analyze the noise in measured intensities and its impact on vector magnetic field mappings.

This study examines the boolean structures arising from involutions in groups, particularly in connection with centralizers and their relationship to p-centralizers when considering p-groups. A key focus is on determining boolean widths for involutions within these p-groups, in a way that mirrors the approach for boolean width in p-groups generally.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves in a 4-dimensional semi-Riemannian manifold do not meet specific geometric criteria. A formula previously established by Bertrand could not be applied to these unique curves, as it requires the satisfaction of an unwarranted condition.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to select the most effective one for a specific task. Despite the widespread belief that the loss function essentially serves as an objective function optimizer, with the goal of minimizing the difference between the predicted and actual outcomes, its true purpose is more complex, according to some sources. In fact, the loss function dictates the learning process by defining how the network's mistakes are calculated and weighted, which in turn affects the learned representations and the ultimate performance of the network on a given task. This paper aims to provide an in-depth examination of the influence that loss function modification can have on the performance of a neural network in a classification context, focusing on three common loss functions: cross-entropy, categorical cross-entropy with a weighting term, and a recently proposed loss function known as soft-label categorical cross-entropy. The results of the experiments conducted on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that loss functions from previous studies that yield biased weighted estimates may yield significantly improved performance when unbiased estimates are employed, casting doubt on the underlying biases hypothesis. The findings also suggest that loss functions that are considered complex may simply be variations of well-known loss functions, and that a loss function that exhibits biased weighted estimates may still yield optimal performance on certain tasks by weighting the importance of different classes.

Our proposed atlas, titled ATOMIC, is an extensive compilation of common knowledge phenomena, consisting of if-then statements that humans have a strong tendency to agree upon.  This atlas differs significantly from other available datasets as ATOMIC categorizes these events into 361 distinct scenarios, further breaking down into 23,821 unique statements.  Notably, we have also included ratings for these statements, obtained through a large-scale survey of 1,052 people, which provides a basis for evaluating the truth of these events.  In recognition of the size and complexity of this atlas, we have implemented a simple evaluation method for assessing the quality of ATOMIC, which yields promising results.  Furthermore, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of incorporating this atlas into existing models for improving their ability to reason and learn from scripts.  In particular, we have observed significant improvements in both image and text recognition tasks following the if-then structure.

Our proposed framework uses a dual representation, comprising a local and a global component, to predict future video frames from an innovative viewpoint. Unlike traditional methods that predict frames from the rearview, our approach predicts frames from a 90-degree rotated viewpoint, presenting numerous challenges and opportunities. We introduce two novel local components, a shallow convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict structure information and a deep CNN to predict texture information, each utilizing a separate local feature map. We also propose a novel global component that utilizes an existing frame rather than the predicted frame, demonstrating its superiority over conventional global components. Our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art results on a real-world dataset, showcasing significant improvements over existing approaches.

A graph G is said to have a property D if there exists a function McD that assigns each point x in G a pair of distinct points (a, b) such that the distance between x and a determines the distance between x and b uniquely, and vice versa. The shortest length at which this property holds true for any point in G is referred to as the minimal width of D in G. We examine the minimal width of the property D in finite graphs, seeking shortest paths of length 2, and we establish a correlation between the property D and the property McD having a shortest path of length 1 or 2.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the varying positions of microphones on devices.  To address these challenges, this study proposes a new method called FD-CNN, which incorporates a feature extraction layer that adapts to the shape of kernels to combat convolutional kernel deformation caused by differing microphone positions.  The study also introduces an innovative way to tackle additive noise by using a noise-aware loss function.  The results, which used a combination of real and simulated data, demonstrate that the proposed FD-CNN approach outperforms current methods for abnormal heart sound detection, showing a high accuracy of 98.6% on a publicly available dataset.  These findings highlight the potential of the proposed technique for creating more accurate cardiac auscultation tools.

Observations of astrophysical systems often rely on assuming that quantum mechanical fluctuations in particle numbers obscure line radiative equilibrium, leading to predictions about spin temperature. Counterintuitively, this assumption might not hold for $^{3}P_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_0$ transitions in $^{3}P_1$ dominant systems, which are crucial for determining spin temperatures and, by extension, gas temperatures. A theoretical analysis indicates that non-equilibrium conditions could significantly impact $^{3}S_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_1$ transition probabilities, potentially forcing new analysis of existing data and guiding observations of the $^{3}P_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_0$ transition to determine the underlying conditions. Confirming or ruling out the importance of non-equilibrium effects could provide a new tool for determining spin temperatures and temperatures more accurately, or potentially validate the use of existing assumptions.

We establish a connection between the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process and a newly defined stochastic process where particles' velocities serve as the focus of interest. By mapping ASEP onto this velocity process, we derive a partial differential equation that describes the distribution function of ASEP's velocity field, and further obtain an explicit formula for the steady-state velocity correlations.

This paper examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to better understand how different scientific disciplines approach epidemic data and make predictions about disease spread. Beginning with an overview of fundamental epidemiological models, we then explore how existing frameworks can be applied to multiple aspects of pandemic data, including case and vaccine data, as well as the challenges of modeling outbreaks across different populations and locations. We also discuss recent developments in statistical learning techniques, highlighting how they can be used to improve existing models and gather valuable information about vulnerable populations. By examining how mathematical models can be used to predict outbreak patterns and guide public health policy, we aim to provide a clear picture of their potential in informing decisions during the pandemic.

Determining whether bulge growth drives the observed turning point in the star formation main sequence for galaxies has been a topic of debate. To explore the role of bulges in shaping the mass-star formation rate (SFR) relationship, a study examined a variety of bulge-to-total light ratio (B/T) definitions and their impact on identifying galaxies with prominent bulges. Unlike previous studies, this research utilized a B/T definition based on stellar masses, accounting for differing evolution rates of bulges and disks. By utilizing this refined B/T classification, analysts found that a smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulation exhibited increased bulge dominance at high stellar masses, aligning with observational data. This shift in B/T ratio correspondence helped explain the turning point in the mass-SFR relationship observed in galaxies, potentially indicating that star formation slows as bulges grow larger and more dominant.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, classifying text as expressing
positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, without using label information during training.
A unified architecture is proposed, combining a sentiment indicator and a sentiment
classifier, which learns jointly across languages. Experimental results demonstrate the
effectiveness of this indicator, with the sentiment classifier performing significantly
better when pre-trained on the proposed indicator versus a baseline. Furthermore,
the paper introduces a novel metric, called "macro-avg. sentiment accuracy per language",
which provides a more comprehensive assessment of sentiment classification. The
suggested approach yields superior sentiment classification accuracy compared to a
standard classification model, across multiple languages and datasets.

A planetary system's formation is influenced by angular momentum conservation, which dictates that momentum remains within the system. As a protoplanetary disk collapses, its flat and vast outer layers slowly converge and settle upon the forming star and planets. This process, spinning up the star and planets in the process, is pivotal in determining how angular momentum is distributed and specialized within the system. A theoretical model has been developed to analyze this phenomenon, focusing on a scenario where a significant planet ingestion event occurs, or alternatively, where a large planet's formation is facilitated by an unexpected transfer of angular momentum. To validate this model, computational simulations were carried out to examine various planetary system configurations, ranging from simple to complex setups, involving both gas and solid planets. In each scenario, the distribution of angular momentum was thoroughly examined and compared to observational data of 10 young stellar systems, including a binary star system and several systems with and without visible planetary debris disks. The results demonstrated that the established theoretical understanding of angular momentum conservation may need to be revised, and it is possible that large-scale planetary formation events could occur through unconventional angular momentum transfers, rather than through the ingestion of massive planets.

False news spreads rapidly on social media platforms, causing consequences for individuals and societies worldwide. The spread of false news is exacerbated by the overwhelming amount of information shared online, making it challenging to quickly identify and correct false information. This research focuses on developing an efficient method to identify emergent false news using multiple sources of information, including text, images, and video. A meta-learning approach was employed to utilize existing true and false news datasets, overcoming the limitation of an insufficient amount of labeled data for training. The existing datasets were used to train a universal model and a news classification model, then the trained models were fine-tuned for true and false news classification. The proposed meta-neural process network (MNPN) outperformed the state-of-the-art results for text, image, and multi-modal false news identification, demonstrating promising potential in real-world applications.

Recently, researchers have explored the concept of complementary sets in signal processing, particularly in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, in a new and exciting way. Complementary sets with a positive integer order $m$ can effectively utilize a spectrum of width $K^m - 1$, and in the case of a one-dimensional complementary set with width $K$, this means generating $K$ signals from a set of $K$ waveform modulators. Although complementary arrays and matrices have been studied extensively in function algebra, the construction methods for higher-order complementary sets are limited and often complicated. A new approach has been introduced, utilizing polynomial extensions and algebraic projections to create sets of high order, which fills this gap and provides a novel perspective on the field. A comprehensive framework has been established for constructing sets of high order with wide spectra, filling a previously unexplored area of research, and presenting immediately applicable construction methods for specific instances of fourth-order complementary sets with wide spectra.

A cutting-edge, highly customizable method for creating simulated brain lesions has been developed, utilizing a progressive pixel-wise variational auto-encoder with an adversarial loss function. This generator network produces realistic lesions by learning from a small sample of annotated data, drawing inspiration from existing lesions within the same image, and employing a multi-scale progressive construction of the lesion area. Evaluations using a small trained model and publicly available data on a standard evaluation dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach, outperforming current techniques in accuracy, without requiring any pre-defined lesion models or Gaussian distributions, and producing usable lesions even when working with healthy brain data.

This paper introduces a novel, universally applicable framework called "Comparative Learning Structure" that incorporates multiple comparative learning techniques, thereby enabling the implementation of comparative learning methods that draw upon features from multiple sources. A major contribution of this paper is the development of an algorithm called "Comparative Learning with Multiple Bi-Embeddings" (CLMBE), which takes advantage of multiple features from different sources by utilizing multiple comparative learning techniques. Theoretical analyses have demonstrated that CLMBE meets the necessary conditions for consistency and optimality. Experimental results have shown that CLMBE outperforms existing comparative learning approaches and achieves performance comparable to deep learning methods, thus demonstrating the effectiveness of comparative learning techniques.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to perform capable actions extending beyond language tasks has created interest in adapting them for use in assistive technologies such as smart canes or hearing aids. An ideal assistive technology based on a language model would accurately interpret and respond to changing environments and user needs. To achieve this, multiple sources of information including visual, audio, and user-input data need to be effectively integrated and utilized by the model. This paper introduces an architecture called Ability, which integrates a language model with a variety of practical skills through training on adapted instruction datasets. The architecture's capabilities are demonstrated by adapting a pre-trained language model to undertake various tasks such as controlling smart home devices, performing health checks using a microscope, and assisting visually impaired individuals through image-based navigation. The paper's results show that the Ability architecture significantly enhances the model's performance on multiple tasks compared to a standalone language model, while also demonstrating reliable and robust performance in real-world settings with a visually impaired individual using image-based navigation.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing the full quantum state of a system is challenging when dealing with its nanoscale components and complex dynamics. While multiple methods are available for state reconstruction, they are often impaired by statistical errors and noise in measurement outcomes. We propose a novel approach using both Wigner and Moyal functions to describe the state of a system, which can provide precise reconstruction of quantum correlations and synchronization dynamics. Our method takes advantage of the fact that the positive semi-definite nature of a quantum state operator is not directly affected by noise or losses in measurement outcomes, which typically pose a major obstacle for state reconstruction. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach by analyzing the reconstruction of quantum synchronization through the steering of entanglement.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module M over a lattice L is generally considered a challenging task. Despite the proposed algorithm by Babai and Kiss in 2000, specifically designed for constructing ideal lattices, constructing the lattice of submodules of M at a given degree n has important applications in various areas of research. Recently, a polynomial-time algorithm was developed to construct the lattice of submodules based on the complete information of the spectrum of the module M, which is not typically available. In contrast, research has shown that constructing the lattice of submodules at a given degree n is possible using only the complete information of the spectrum of all modules M$\downarrow_G$ for subgroups H of G with [H:G:] = 1. This research aims to bridge the aforementioned gap by employing the aforementioned recent advances in constructive dimension theory and the existing algorithm by Babai and Kiss to construct the lattice of submodules of a given module M at a degree n based on the partial information of its spectrum.

We explore how certain repetitive operators affect biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space, with a focus on their implications for their mean curvature. A key aspect of our research involves examining the predictive potential of these operators for identifying biharmonic hypersurfaces with negative mean curvature. Our findings demonstrate that only a limited set of biharmonic hypersurfaces satisfy this condition, as it generally requires their embeddedness within a 3-dimensional Euclidean space. Moreover, we observe that any biharmonic hypersurface within a 3-dimensional Euclidean space that is minimized will have negative mean curvature. Our investigation also delves into the classification of biharmonic hypersurfaces based on their mean curvature, as well as the identification of all possible minimal biharmonic hypersurfaces within the 3-dimensional Euclidean space.

A set is identifiable through a ratio $p/q$ if its characteristic vector is uniquely determined by the vector of ratios into which its elements are divided by a given ratio $p/q$. We establish that a set $S$ is identifiable through a ratio $p/q$ if and only if there exists a bijection $\phi$ that partitions its elements based on their structure in the network and maps them into distinct intervals so that elements within the same connected component of the network's subgraph induced by $S$ are integrated into the same interval under $\phi$.

We perform a systematic analysis of the factors influencing the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate, focusing on the shape of the angular distribution and the transverse momentum ($p_T$) of the muon. Our study reveals that the leading contributions from the decay operator and the weak interaction are already accounted for by the existing description. We then examine various theoretical aspects, including: the impact of the form factor corrections on the rate and spectrum; the relationship between the $p_T$ distribution and the form factors; the significance of the spinor normalization; the role of higher-order effects from the decay operator; and the contribution from the decay constant of the $D_s^-$ meson. Our findings indicate that the current theoretical understanding is sufficient to describe the decay process, and that additional factors such as QED corrections and weak annihilation will have a negligible influence on the result.

A series of experiments was conducted to investigate the auditory characteristics of a tape unrolling under varying tension conditions, with or without an applied static horizontal force, by recording both the sound and the resulting velocity profiles. The analysis focused on the onset of sticking failure, marked by a sharp increase in sound intensity, which was found to precede the onset of significant sticking failure velocity. The results demonstrate that the sound intensity and the sticking failure onset time are directly correlated, indicating that the sound contains information about the sticking failure progression. A simple model was employed to explain the observed patterns, suggesting that the sound intensity reflects the formation of localized stress concentrations that ultimately lead to failure. The research provides evidence for a self-organizing process behind the noisy signals emitted during the tape unrolling, with a proposed power law relationship between sound intensity and sticking failure time constant. The findings have implications for developing signal processing techniques to improve failure time constant estimation.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an extension of the concept of metric spaces, introducing the idea of "segment spaces" and subsequently "angle spaces". These structures are characterized by a relation called "betweenness", mimicking the role of lines in geometric spaces. Menger's work was motivated by the desire to generalize certain metric properties, yet in his initial presentation, he identified two problems posed by M. Fr\'echet that he was unable to resolve. The first issue involves determining whether in a straight line space over a set S, the "triangle inequality" is necessarily satisfied for all distance functions. The second problem asks whether the triangle inequality is inherent in a way S is structured, given that it holds for all distance functions defined on S. In this paper, we provide solutions to these two problems by demonstrating that the triangle inequality naturally arises from the "segment function" structure alone.

Our proposed TPC: Point Cloud smoothing algorithm shows that adding random points via bbox-based bbox-trimming bbox-expansion and bbox-movement techniques surpasses existing methods by 30% in preserving unique transformations of tree structures, without significantly increasing the point cloud size, which in one case increases by 0.2%

This study develops a geometric framework to evaluate programs based on their output spaces, incorporating tools from algebraic geometry, specifically from the perspective of computational learning. A key component of this framework is a constructive method for defining the output space of a program, which can be considered as the "image" of its input space under the program's computational processes, in the form of a geometric variety. A key benefit of this approach is the derivation of measures for the output space's "complexity," which can be utilized in evaluating programs based on simplicity criteria, such as those originating from constructive logic. Moreover, this framework provides a straightforward method for identifying and characterizing "overfitting" situations in learning programs, which can't be defined in traditional function-based models.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the conjecture proposed by Grothendieck, relating to the description of local components of representations of the algebraic fundamental group for curves over p-adic fields, specifically for curves of genus 1. Our argument revolves around the application of relative Kummer theory in an abelian variety, which enables us to identify and describe certain components of these representations. In the process, we derive clear information about the weights of these components, which serves as the primary contribution of our work.

This study proposes a new method for accurately identifying damage in self-sensing composites using Genetic Algorithms in conjunction with Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) imaging. Unlike existing research that focuses on reconstructing healthy or unhealthy states, this technique aims to precisely map damage within the composite by analyzing variations in electrical resistance. A key innovation of this research is the development of a new fitness function that accounts for the physical limitations of composite materials, leading to more accurate damage identification. A 2D finite element model was employed to validate the method's accuracy by comparing reconstruction results from Genetic Algorithms and real-time EIT imaging. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed approach can accurately identify damage in self-sensing composites based on resistance changes, overcoming the limitations of current imaging techniques and providing a promising foundation for future applications in monitoring composite materials under real-time loading conditions.

This work examines the geometric measures that can be applied to the construction of a tensor representation of a Euclidean space. A Euclidean space can be defined as a vector space over the real numbers with an inner product, enabling the measurement of distance and angle. A key aspect of this study involves analyzing how geometric measures relate to the tensor representation of a Euclidean space, specifically in terms of inner products and metrics. A key finding shows that the tensor representation of a Euclidean space is essentially indistinguishable from the representation based on geometric measures, highlighting their equivalence. Consequently, this research demonstrates that the geometric measures of a Euclidean space can be determined from the underlying vector space, eliminating the need for a metric or inner product in its definition.

A right-angled Artin group is a type of group that has received significant mathematical attention, and its structure can be understood by analyzing its graph associated with a given set of relations. A key component of this structure are divisions of the graph, which have a direct impact on the subgroup hierarchy within the group. Specifically, we have the following findings: any finitely generated subgroup of a right-angled Artin group on a connected graph will intersect only finitely many vertex groups, and this intersection structure is essentially the same as the structure of its subgroups of largest rank, as well as its closed subgroups of finite index, in a equivalent variation of the well-known Kurosh subgroup theorem.

The development of GPU-accelerated computers has enabled the creation of large-scale numerical simulations, which often require solving systems of linear equations and computing matrix inverses. While iterative methods like Sherman-Morrison and Woodbury are commonly used for this purpose, they are not well-suited for GPU architectures due to their slow convergence in many cases. This study introduces generalized formulas for (n-1)-order iterative matrix inversion, which can be applied in scenarios where a submatrix's inverse is known. These formulas outperform existing higher-order methods by significantly reducing memory usage and can be optimized for GPU execution. In certain scenarios with specific input distributions, these methods may even achieve better time performance.

Contextual linear Gibbs distribued gamits is an interesting concept for modeling behavioral data, especially in environments that are privacy-conscious and/or distributed. Unlike traditional linear regression, this model type takes into account the variability of data, utilizing a Gaussian distribution to represent the parameter. Although contextual information is not shared among components in this model, it is essential to determine the context that leads to significant variations. Determining this variance is crucial for updating the parameter in an efficient manner, particularly during Bayesian learning. A novel approach has been developed to compute the variance of the context, utilizing only a combination of the contextual values and the IDs of data points, as opposed to the actual data. This technique results in significantly reduced communication costs when distributing the model across multiple machines, and further contributes to the development of an efficient learning algorithm that synchronizes the context variance across components.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) affects the rotation of gases in protoplanetary disk systems, particularly in their outer regions, by generating waves and/or oscillations. While this instability might contribute to the development of dust particles in these areas, its stabilization or destabilization can be influenced by the presence of dust, which affects how heat is distributed within the atmosphere. Determining the effects of dust growth on VSI stability is crucial for understanding its role in shaping these systems, as well as its impact on planetary formation and development.

This research focuses on a key aspect of geometric analysis involving partial differential equations, specifically the Liouville theorem for a particular type of manifold with diminishing Ricci curvature and constant scalar curvature. A substantial contribution of this work is the derivation of the Liouville theorem under the mentioned conditions, along with an enhancement of previous results by Yau, Schoen, and Gao-Fang. Furthermore, we utilize the obtained Liouville theorem to solve several complex problems and establish new insights in various areas of mathematics, including calculus of variations, geometric analysis, and theoretical physics. The paper's findings have significant implications for understanding the qualitative properties of solutions to certain partial differential equations, particularly the Yasui-Yau decomposition theorem, the Bochner-Weitzenb\"ock formula, and the famous Witten genus equation in geometric analysis and theoretical physics.

Recent advancements in vision transformers have led to success in various tasks, but local computations within transformers pose a performance challenge when using large kernels. This issue is particularly pronounced when employing dynamic kernel sizes, which are highly desirable for tasks like image classification where different categories of images may be distinguished by distinct patterns at various scales. Implementing dynamic kernels with existing transformer architectures is complicated due to the necessity of adapting the kernel size to the input data, which requires significant computational efforts. In response, a new approach called Dynamic Entrances with Global Mean Pooling has been developed, which enables the use of large kernels without the burden of extensive computation. This method involves placing multiple entrance points throughout the input data, which are then treated as separate inputs, allowing the single transformer layer to process data of any size without the need for extensive adaptation. As a result, a single Dynamic Entrances with Global Mean Pooling layer can effectively handle data of any size, eliminating the necessity for multiple layers to achieve this goal. The proposed technique yields notable improvements over traditional approaches like local embedding and achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.

In the context of learning from diverse data, a current challenge is achieving fast convergence for parameters. This paper introduces an optimized algorithm called 'Stroll for Education' that addresses this issue. This algorithm combines a random walk with gradient descent and utilizes local optimality conditions to streamline the search for a better learning rate. The authors' proposed technique enhances the existing adaptive random walk method by using a more efficient search strategy. The 'Stroll for Education' algorithm outperforms other notable algorithms, specifically SGD with momentum and ADAGRAD, in various educational datasets and scenarios, including single-device and federated learning setups.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This technique has several advantages over alternative approaches such as adversarial and generative methods. The proposed technique uses existing libraries of interpolation functions such as nearest neighbor and linear interpolation. It can be implemented using a few lines of code, making it an attractive option for semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local effect resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously describing it as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-local effect of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over the particle's separation, allowing the party to be influenced or have its state determined through the party whose state is intentionally manipulated. Consequently, despite single-particle entanglement not violating the no-action principle, the resulting spreading of the wave function results in the phenomenon of steering, as well as other non-local effects, according to quantum mechanics.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper provides an exhaustive review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive analysis paves the way for developing a new Blockchain-supported FL framework that incorporates intelligent driving systems, meets the specific needs of IoVs, and contributes to the development of a personalized intelligent driving ecosystem.

A deep learning model such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is widely used for video identification, yet its large size and high computational requirements pose a significant challenge for real-time processing. This paper presents an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to create an energy-efficient LSTM model, targeting video identification tasks. The report outlines the design of a low-power LSTM accelerator, utilizing a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition to reduce model size and optimize memory usage. The authors' novel fractional tensor decompositions and optimized hardware architectures also enhance computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, with the designed accelerator outperforming existing deep learning accelerators and achieving real-time video identification on a variety of datasets.

This study examines the connection between the prime factors of a natural number expressed in base b, and the cycles of iterated composite functions. A direct correspondence is established between prime factors and cycle structures, illustrating how specific factorizations yield distinct cycle patterns when applying a given composite function repeatedly. A notable case involves a bijective function f defined as the iteration of two primitive functions, for which research has been conducted on its cycle behavior. In this notable case, a direct link is found between the prime factorization of integers, specifically their distance from a base point under f, and their cycle behavior when applied to the integer input.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions exponentially increase within a finite time frame in the same higher-dimensional space, assuming they do so initially. This expansion solution cannot be sustained in a solution that declines as $r^m$ or better in a neighborhood around infinity, where $m$ is any negative value. Furthermore, we conclude that a homogenous radial solution is optimal under the focusing mass-supercritical Ginzburg-Landau equation in a 3D space, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle, assuming it satisfies a certain symmetry property and a stability condition.

We provide a proof that local uniform deduction properties hold for varieties defined over the integers, when the characteristic of the underlying field is positive, by connecting semi-parametric local uniform deduction properties to semi-decidability, in the context of finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras.

Comparative evaluations of statistical models have sparked a debate over the use of Bayes factors, with some employing single-point estimates of the model evidence and others utilizing the entire posterior distribution of the evidence. We contend that the method of evaluating Bayes factors is not a one-time choice, as it can significantly impact outcomes and influence the development of models. We explore various strategies for employing Bayes factors in a subjective and objective manner, considering both local and global optimizations, as well as utilizing sampling methods such as importance sampling and bridge sampling. We demonstrate that drawing a random sample from the posterior distribution of the model evidence may not yield an accurate estimate of the Bayes factor, illustrating the importance of local optimization. We also introduce an algorithm for mapping the posterior distribution of the Bayes factor, allowing researchers to visualize its behavior and identify areas of high accuracy for single-point estimates. We conclude that choosing an appropriate method for evaluating Bayes factors is crucial for making informed decisions about model comparison, drawing on a variety of techniques including Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation, Bayesian model averaging, and the use of prior distributions of model parameters.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate how discourse indicators contribute to the representation of sentences in classification tasks. Existing studies have established correlations between discourse indicators and sentence representations but are limited to specific instances and indicators. In contrast, discourse indicators vary greatly and their relationships are complex. To rectify this, the paper utilizes existing classification models to predict discourse indicators between sentences with established semantic links in multiple datasets and examines the underlying mechanisms of discourse indicators in sentence representations. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the roles discourse indicators play in capturing semantic connections between sentences.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a one-parameter group representation for both classical and quantum Jordanian de Formes models. The resulting representation is essentially a composition of the classical and quantum Jordanian de Formes models, mirrored in their respective frameworks.
